overview.title: 📖 Overview: Courtyard Houses and the Levites' Special Standing
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 33a–33b
overview.hebrewSource: בָּתֵּי הַחֲצֵרִים נוֹתְנִין לָהֶם כֹּחַ יָפֶה שֶׁבְּבָתֵּי עָרֵי חוֹמָה וְכֹחַ יָפֶה שֶׁבַּשָּׂדוֹת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes out the historical digression about the land's sanctity and turns to a third category of dwelling: houses in unwalled courtyards (villages too small to count as true walled cities), which combine advantageous rules from both fields and walled-city houses. The Gemara works out exactly how those rules combine, especially for a consecrated courtyard-house redeemed by someone other than the owner. It then defines precisely which places qualify as 'unwalled courtyards,' before turning to the Levites' unique, permanent right to redeem their houses and fields at any time — a right so strong the Gemara must work out exactly which of a Levite's relatives can inherit it.

slides.title: 🏡 New Mishna: The Best of Both Worlds
slides.subtitle: Houses in unwalled courtyards borrow rules from two other categories
rows: May be redeemed immediately and throughout the first twelve months
Leave the buyer's possession at the Jubilee Year, OR by a per-annum deduction from the price
Unlike fields, no two-year minimum wait before redemption — derived from 'redemption shall be his,' immediately
Unlike walled-city houses, never become the buyer's permanently after a year — they always return by the Jubilee

callout.label: Source:
callout.text: Leviticus 25:31 explicitly juxtaposes unwalled-courtyard houses to 'the fields of the country' — inheriting the field's Jubilee-return rule while keeping the walled-house's immediate redeemability.

slides.title: 🔙 A Consecrated Courtyard-House: Does It Ever Come Home?
slides.subtitle: Rav Huna and Rabbi Oshaya disagree about what happens when someone ELSE redeems it from hekdesh

lines.speaker: Rav Huna
lines.text: The phrase 'and it shall go out in the Jubilee' is specifically needed for: an owner consecrates his courtyard-house, ANOTHER person redeems it from the Temple treasury, and the Jubilee arrives. Result: it returns to the ORIGINAL owner — neither locked to the redeemer (like a walled house) nor lost to the priests (like a field).

lines.speaker: R' Oshaya
lines.text: Not so — 'he gives the money and it stands assured to him' (Lev. 27:19) means whoever redeems consecrated property owns it fully and finally, in every category.

lines.speaker: Rav Zeira's challenge
lines.text: Why require that ANOTHER redeemed it first? Shouldn't an unredeemed courtyard-house simply return to the owner at the Jubilee regardless?

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: No — an utterly unredeemed house never leaves hekdesh 'for free'; that would let people say consecrated property exits without any redemption at all.

callout.label: The verdict:
callout.text: A later baraita is found stating Rav Huna's position explicitly, refuting Rabbi Oshaya.

slides.title: 📜 What Counts as 'Houses of Unwalled Courtyards'?
slides.subtitle: New mishna: a small settlement can qualify — even behind an ancient wall

steps.content: 1️⃣ Minimum size: two courtyards, each containing two houses — derived from the plural 'houses' and plural 'courtyards' in Lev. 25:31

2️⃣ Surprisingly: even a place that IS surrounded by a wall from Joshua's era still counts as 'unwalled' if it's this small — the verse's 'which have no wall' teaches that size can override an actual wall
3️⃣ Why not just 'a house and a courtyard' (one each)? The Torah could have written 'courtyards' alone if a single house sufficed — 'houses' in the plural is deliberate

slides.title: 🕎 A Levite's Perpetual Right of Redemption
slides.subtitle: New mishna: even inheritance across tribal lines has its own rules

nodes.content: ❓ An Israelite inherits a walled-city house from his LEVITE grandfather — does he redeem it 'always' like a Levite, or only within the standard one year?
📜 Rebbi: the perpetual right requires BOTH conditions — the seller must be a Levite AND the house must be in a Levite city (Lev. 25:32-33)

columns.label: Rebbi's ruling
columns.content: This Israelite grandson redeems only within one year, like any Israelite — he lacks the 'Levite' half of the requirement

columns.label: The Rabbis' ruling
columns.content: Any inheritor of a Levite-city house redeems it perpetually, Levite or not — location alone suffices

nodes.content: ⚠️ Excluded even under the lenient reading: a Levite who is a mamzer or Gibeonite-born — disqualified from the community, so not 'a Levite' for this purpose

slides.title: 🏛️ Levite Cities: Fields, Lots, and Open Land
slides.subtitle: A different mishna protects the Levites' surrounding open land
slides.label: The rule:
slides.text: In Levite cities, one may not convert a field into an open lot (migrash), an open lot into a field, part of the city into open land, or open land into city — the boundaries are frozen. Rabbi Elazar limits this rigidity to Levite cities specifically; in ordinary Israelite cities, one MAY convert a field into a lot or a lot into part of the city (just not the reverse), precisely so that Israelite cities can keep growing rather than shrinking. Priests and Levites, meanwhile, may sell and redeem their fields and houses always — 'the Levites shall have a perpetual right of redemption' (Lev. 25:32) — overriding the two-year field rule, the Jubilee-forfeiture-to-priests rule, and the one-year walled-house rule, all at once.

summary.principle: Houses in unwalled courtyards blend the immediate redeemability of walled-city houses with a field's ultimate return at the Jubilee, while Levites enjoy an even stronger, truly perpetual right to redeem their property at any time — a privilege the Gemara carefully bounds by exactly who counts as the seller and where the property sits.

flowSteps.content: 🏡 Courtyard houses: redeemable immediately (like walled houses), but always return by the Jubilee (like fields)
🔙 If consecrated and redeemed by another, Rav Huna: it still returns to the original owner at the Jubilee

columns.content: 📜 Qualifying as 'unwalled': just two courtyards of two houses each — even behind a real ancient wall
🕎 A Levite's perpetual redemption right requires both a Levite seller AND a Levite city (per Rebbi)

flowSteps.content: 🏛️ Levite cities freeze field/lot/city boundaries; Israelite cities may still grow
🎓 Key Principle: the Torah calibrates three separate tiers of redemption rights — ordinary fields, walled houses, and the Levites' permanent claim — each protecting a different kind of vulnerability

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, how do houses of unwalled courtyards combine the rules of fields and walled-city houses?
o: They follow only the rules of fields, with no borrowing from walled-city houses
They may be redeemed immediately like walled-city houses, but they always return to the seller at the Jubilee like fields — never becoming permanently the buyer's
They may never be redeemed under any circumstances
They follow only the rules of walled-city houses
quiz.e: The mishna gives courtyard houses the walled-city house's immediate redeemability while keeping the ancestral field's Jubilee-return protection — the best (for the seller) of both categories.

quiz.q: According to Rav Huna, what happens when someone consecrates a courtyard-house, ANOTHER person redeems it from the Temple treasury, and the Jubilee Year then arrives unredeemed by the original owner?
o: It permanently belongs to the person who redeemed it from hekdesh
It goes to the priests, exactly like an unredeemed ancestral field
It returns to the original owner at the Jubilee — neither locked to the redeemer nor lost to the priests
It remains with the Temple treasury forever
quiz.e: Rav Huna teaches that this specific case is why the verse needed to add 'it shall go out in the Jubilee' — the house returns to its original owner, unlike either a walled-city house (which locks to the buyer) or a field (which passes to the priests).

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, how small can a settlement be and still qualify as 'houses of unwalled courtyards' — even if it happens to have an ancient wall from Joshua's era?
o: It must have at least ten houses
As few as two courtyards, each containing two houses
Any single house counts, regardless of courtyards
It must have no wall of any kind, ever, under any circumstance
quiz.e: The Gemara derives from the plural terms 'houses' and 'courtyards' in Leviticus 25:31 that a minimum of two courtyards of two houses each qualifies as an unwalled-courtyard settlement — even overriding the presence of an actual ancient wall.

quiz.q: According to Rebbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) in the new mishna, what two conditions must BOTH be met for a house to be redeemable perpetually under the Levite's special right?
o: The house must be expensive and located in Jerusalem
The seller must be a Levite AND the house must be located in a city of the Levites
The house must be a courtyard house and consecrated
Only that the buyer must be an Israelite
quiz.e: Rebbi derives from the verse's wording that the perpetual redemption right applies only when both conditions hold together — a Levite seller and a Levite city — so an Israelite who merely inherited such a house from a Levite grandfather does not get the perpetual right.

quiz.q: Why does Rabbi Elazar limit the rule against converting fields into open lots (or vice versa) to Levite cities specifically?
o: Because Israelite cities have no open lots at all
Because in Israelite cities such conversions ARE permitted in the direction of city growth (field to lot, lot to city), so the cities are not stunted
Because Levite cities never had any fields to begin with
Because the rule applies equally everywhere with no distinction
quiz.e: Rabbi Elazar explains that in ordinary Israelite cities, conversions that allow the city to expand (field to lot, lot to city) are permitted specifically so that Israelite settlements are not prevented from growing — only Levite cities keep the strict, symmetric prohibition in both directions.
